lessonTitle: Occupational and Environmental Health: Histories, Diseases and the Hierarchy of Controls

blocks.text: A 71-year-old retired shipyard worker is seen with progressive breathlessness. A chest X-ray shows pleural thickening. He has seen four doctors in two years; none asked what he did for a living in the 1970s. Many occupational diseases are diagnosed only when someone asks one simple question: 'What work have you done, and what were you exposed to?'

blocks.markdown: **The occupational history.** Work is a cause or contributor in a large share of respiratory, skin, musculoskeletal, hearing and mental health problems, yet it is easily overlooked. The occupational history should be a routine part of the social history, and in suspected work-related illness it should be detailed and chronological, covering every job.

items: Current job: job title, employer, what the person actually does, hours and shifts
Exposures: dusts, fumes, chemicals, noise, vibration, biological agents, manual handling, repetitive tasks, psychosocial stress
Controls: ventilation, enclosure, protective equipment, training, health surveillance

Time course: when symptoms began, and whether they improve at weekends or on holiday and recur on return (the strongest clue to work-relatedness; also distinguish work-related disease, caused by work, from work-aggravated disease, a pre-existing condition worsened by work)
Others affected: colleagues with similar symptoms
Previous jobs: job titles, duration, exposures (important for diseases with long latency such as asbestos-related disease)
Non-work exposures: hobbies, home environment, smoking

blocks.markdown: **Common occupational diseases.** *Occupational asthma* is caused by a workplace sensitiser (for example flour dust or isocyanates) and is diagnosed partly by serial peak flow recordings at and away from work and by specialist assessment. *Asbestos-related diseases* (pleural plaques, asbestosis, mesothelioma, lung cancer) arise after a latency that is typically decades. *Silicosis* follows inhalation of silica dust (quarrying, stone cutting). *Noise-induced hearing loss* is gradual and begins with loss at high frequencies. *Hand-arm vibration syndrome* follows use of vibrating tools and causes vascular and neurological symptoms in the fingers. *Occupational contact dermatitis* occurs in hairdressers, cleaners, caterers and health workers. Musculoskeletal disorders and work-related stress are the commonest causes of work-related ill health overall. In the UK, employers have duties under health and safety legislation, including the Control of Substances Hazardous to Health (COSHH) regulations, and certain diseases and injuries must be reported (RIDDOR); check current Health and Safety Executive (HSE) guidance.

rows: Eliminate or substitute the sensitiser; local exhaust ventilation; early recognition and removal from exposure
Do not disturb asbestos; licensed removal; compensation and long-term follow-up
Reduce noise at source; enclosure; hearing protection; audiometric surveillance
Lower-vibration tools; limit exposure time; health surveillance
Reduce wet work; gloves; skin care; substitution of irritants
blocks.caption: Examples only; consult current HSE guidance for legal duties and exposure limits.

blocks.markdown: **Quantifying exposure.** Noise exposure is expressed as an A-weighted level in decibels, dB(A). Because the decibel is logarithmic, every 3 dB increase doubles the sound energy. To compare exposures of different durations, the equivalent continuous level over a reference period of 8 hours is used (assuming negligible exposure for the rest of the period):

blocks.caption: $L$ is the constant sound level in dB(A) and $t$ the exposure time in hours. UK regulations set action values for daily or weekly exposure; check current HSE guidance.

blocks.title: Daily noise exposure
blocks.prompt: A machine operator is exposed to a constant 95 dB(A) for 4 hours of an 8-hour shift and negligible noise otherwise. Calculate the 8-hour equivalent level.

steps.text: Halving the time lowers the level by about 3 dB, so the daily level is about 92 dB(A). This is above commonly used action values, so the employer must control the noise and offer hearing protection and health surveillance (check current HSE levels).

blocks.markdown: **Attributable risk in exposed workers.** Occupational epidemiology often asks what proportion of disease in exposed workers is due to the exposure. If the relative risk is $RR$, the attributable fraction among the exposed is:

blocks.caption: Assumes the association is causal and unconfounded.

blocks.title: Proportion of disease due to exposure
blocks.prompt: In a cohort study of stonemasons, the relative risk of a lung disease is 5 compared with unexposed workers. What proportion of cases in the exposed workers is attributable to the exposure?

steps.text: Interpretation: 80% of cases among exposed stonemasons would not have occurred in the absence of the exposure, if the association is causal and there is no confounding, such as from smoking.
Use: the figure strengthens the case for prevention and for compensation schemes, and shows why exposure control is the priority.

blocks.answer: 80%, assuming a causal and unconfounded association.

blocks.markdown: **The hierarchy of controls.** Hazards are controlled most reliably by removing them rather than by relying on people's behaviour. The hierarchy runs from the most to the least effective: **elimination** (remove the hazard), **substitution** (replace with something less hazardous), **engineering controls** (isolate people from the hazard, for example enclosures and local exhaust ventilation), **administrative controls** (change the way people work: rotation, training, signage, limiting exposure time, health surveillance) and, last, **personal protective equipment (PPE)**. PPE is last because it depends on correct selection, fit and use, and it does not remove the hazard.

rows: Redesign the process so that no solvent is needed
Use a water-based cleaner instead of a solvent-based one
Spray booth with local exhaust ventilation; machine enclosure
Job rotation; training; limiting time in noisy areas
Respirators, ear defenders, gloves, used when other controls are insufficient
blocks.caption: Higher levels are more effective and less dependent on behaviour.

blocks.title: Taking an occupational history
blocks.prompt: A 34-year-old baker reports wheeze and nasal symptoms that began 6 months after starting work and settle at weekends. How would you take the history and what would you do?

steps.text: Ask for a full job description: the tasks, exposure to flour dust and additives, ventilation, protective equipment and any colleagues with symptoms.
Define the temporal pattern: ask when the symptoms start in the shift, how they change on days off and on holiday, and whether they recur on return.
Request serial peak flow recordings several times a day over weeks at work and away from work, and arrange early specialist review if occupational asthma is suspected; check current guidance.

Discuss with the patient what exposure control is possible and the implications for his employment; occupational health and the employer have a role, and early removal from exposure improves outcomes.

blocks.answer: History establishes a work-related pattern; objective monitoring and specialist review follow, with exposure control.

points: Take an occupational history as part of every social history, covering all jobs, exposures, controls, time course and colleagues.
Common occupational diseases include occupational asthma, asbestos-related disease, noise-induced hearing loss, hand-arm vibration syndrome and contact dermatitis; some have long latency.
Quantify exposure: the equivalent continuous noise level uses a logarithmic scale; attributable fraction among the exposed is (RR - 1)/RR.
The hierarchy of controls: elimination, substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls, then PPE as the last resort.

questions.stem: A patient has recurrent wheeze that you suspect may be work-related. Which question is most useful in judging work-relatedness?

options.text: Do you have any allergies to penicillin?
How many siblings do you have?
Do your symptoms improve on days off or on holiday and recur on return to work?
What is your date of birth?

questions.correctOptionText: Do your symptoms improve on days off or on holiday and recur on return to work?

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: not relevant to work-related wheeze.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: a temporal pattern linked to work is the strongest clue.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this does not relate to work.

questions.explanation: Symptoms that improve away from work and worsen on return are the typical pattern of work-related illness such as occupational asthma. This temporal pattern is the starting point for further objective assessment.

questions.stem: Which statement about asbestos-related disease is correct?

options.text: There is typically a latency of several decades between exposure and the development of mesothelioma
Mesothelioma typically appears within weeks of exposure
Only people who currently work with asbestos can be affected
Asbestos exposure is not associated with lung cancer

questions.correctOptionText: There is typically a latency of several decades between exposure and the development of mesothelioma

distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this is much too short.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: historic exposure is important, and household exposure can occur.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: asbestos increases the risk of lung cancer.

questions.explanation: Asbestos-related diseases are characterised by very long latency, so the occupational history must cover jobs held decades earlier. This is why a retired worker may present long after the exposure ended.

questions.stem: A factory replaces a solvent-based degreasing agent with a water-based cleaner. At which level of the hierarchy of controls does this act?

options.text: Elimination
Personal protective equipment
Administrative controls
Substitution

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: elimination would remove the need for the degreasing step entirely.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: PPE protects the individual without changing the hazard.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: administrative controls change working practices rather than the agent.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: replacing a hazardous agent with a safer one is substitution.

questions.explanation: Substitution replaces a hazard with a less hazardous alternative, and sits second in the hierarchy. If the degreasing step could be removed altogether, that would be elimination.

questions.stem: According to the hierarchy of controls, which control is generally the most effective?

options.text: Using warning signs
Eliminating the hazard
Providing personal protective equipment
Giving workers training

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: signs are administrative and the least reliable.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: removing the hazard is the most reliable.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: PPE is the last resort.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: training is an administrative control that depends on behaviour.

questions.explanation: Controls that remove or contain the hazard work independently of human behaviour and are therefore more reliable than controls that depend on people following procedures. PPE is considered last because it depends on correct fit and use.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old forestry worker who uses chainsaws daily reports episodes in which his fingertips go white and numb in the cold, with tingling. Which diagnosis and preventive approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Noise-induced hearing loss; avoid cold
Occupational contact dermatitis; use emollients only
Hand-arm vibration syndrome; reduce vibration exposure through lower-vibration tools, limiting exposure time and health surveillance
Occupational asthma; wear a mask

questions.correctOptionText: Hand-arm vibration syndrome; reduce vibration exposure through lower-vibration tools, limiting exposure time and health surveillance

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: hearing loss does not cause finger blanching.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: dermatitis does not cause blanching of the fingers.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: vascular and neurological finger symptoms with vibrating tool use indicate hand-arm vibration syndrome.

questions.explanation: Episodic white, numb fingers in a worker who uses vibrating tools suggest hand-arm vibration syndrome. Prevention follows the hierarchy: lower-vibration tools, limits on exposure time and health surveillance, with early recognition to prevent progression.

questions.stem: A worker is exposed to a constant 100 dB(A) for 1 hour during an 8-hour shift, with negligible noise otherwise. Using L(Aeq,8h) = L + 10 log10(t/8), calculate the 8-hour equivalent continuous level in dB(A), to one decimal place.
questions.explanation: The ratio t/8 is 1/8 = 0.125, and log10(0.125) = -0.903, so 10 x (-0.903) = -9.03. Adding to 100 gives 90.97, which rounds to 91.0 dB(A). The result shows that short bursts of very loud noise still produce a high daily exposure.

questions.stem: In a cohort of foundry workers, the relative risk of a respiratory disease is 4 compared with unexposed workers. Calculate the attributable fraction among the exposed, as a percentage, assuming the association is causal.
questions.explanation: The attributable fraction among the exposed is (RR - 1)/RR = (4 - 1)/4 = 0.75, or 75%. This means three quarters of cases among exposed workers would be prevented if the exposure were removed, provided the association is causal and not confounded.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old hairdresser attends with an itchy, cracked rash on both hands that is worse during the working week. Describe how you would take an occupational history and how you would advise on prevention.
markingGuide: Job description: tasks, products used (shampoos, colours, perming solutions), amount of wet work, glove use and type, hand-washing frequency
Time course: onset, improvement on days off or on holiday, recurrence on return
Other exposures: home tasks, hobbies, atopy history, colleagues with similar symptoms
Previous jobs and exposures
Examination of the hands and other skin; consider patch testing via a specialist
Prevention: reduce wet work, suitable gloves, skin care and moisturisers, substitution of sensitisers, workplace controls
Occupational health and employer input; impact on work and reporting duties (check current HSE guidance)
questions.explanation: A good answer pairs a structured, chronological history (with temporal pattern and product exposures) with prevention based on reducing exposure. Linking to the employer and occupational health shows awareness of workplace responsibility.

questions.stem: A workshop uses a spray painting process that releases solvent vapour and isocyanate-containing mist. Apply the hierarchy of controls to propose measures, in order of effectiveness, and explain why personal protective equipment is last.
markingGuide: Elimination: change the process so that spraying is unnecessary, for example a different coating method
Substitution: use a lower-hazard paint, such as water-based paint
Engineering: spray booth with local exhaust ventilation, enclosure, automation
Administrative: limit exposure time, rotate tasks, training, health surveillance including symptom and lung function monitoring
PPE: correctly fitted respiratory protective equipment as the last line of defence
Why PPE is last: relies on correct selection, fit, maintenance and use; does not remove the hazard; protects only the wearer
Monitoring effectiveness and legal duties (COSHH); check current HSE guidance
questions.explanation: The hierarchy ranks controls by their reliability and their independence from human behaviour. A strong answer proposes measures at several levels and explains why PPE alone is inadequate.

questions.stem: Describe noise-induced hearing loss: how it arises, how it presents, and how it can be prevented in workers.
markingGuide: Cause: prolonged or repeated exposure to loud noise damages hair cells in the cochlea
Presentation: gradual, bilateral, high-frequency loss at first, difficulty hearing in noisy environments, tinnitus
Diagnosis: occupational history and audiometry showing a characteristic notch
Prevention using the hierarchy: reduce noise at source, enclosure, quieter machinery, limit exposure time, hearing protection
Health surveillance with periodic audiometry; employer duties under noise regulations (check current HSE action values)
Irreversible damage, so prevention and early detection are key
questions.explanation: The answer should connect mechanism (cochlear damage) to presentation (high-frequency loss) and then to prevention by the hierarchy of controls with surveillance. Irreversibility is the reason prevention is emphasised.
